overview.title: Learn
overview.intro: When you can’t place a digit, look for a candidate you can cross out. A few removals can leave a cell with only one choice.
difficultyParagraphs: Beginner, Easy, Medium, Tricky, Hard, Very Hard, Expert, Master, Extreme, and Impossible form our learning path. Medium is the starting difficulty for new players. Each level includes the techniques from earlier levels.
A difficulty describes the techniques used to solve a puzzle. Repeating an easy technique does not raise its level. Every level has one puzzle quality standard, with no separate workload setting.

Beginner focuses on visual scanning. Easy adds all singles. Medium introduces local candidate removals. Tricky follows one digit across houses, and Hard introduces wings. Very Hard starts chains and coloring; Expert and Master build general and grouped chains. Extreme combines forcing proofs and specialist patterns.
Impossible is our highest level. A skilled person may still solve these puzzles, but a practical human solution is not promised. Some may need extensive case analysis or computer help.

Articles follow the course order below. A family article can include later extensions, which are marked by their practice difficulty. You can return to those extensions after learning their prerequisites.
overview.fundamentalsNote: For the rules, cell addresses, and candidates, start with

fundamentals.title: Fundamentals
fundamentals.summary: Read a cell address and work out which digits can go there.

paragraphs: Pick an empty cell with several placed digits in its row, column, or box. Cross off every digit those three houses already contain.
If one digit remains, you can place it. If several remain, try a cell whose houses contain more distinct digits.
A house is a row, a column, or a 3×3 box. Thick lines mark the boxes. Each house must contain the digits 1 through 9 once each. The digits you start with are called givens, or clues.
Every cell belongs to three houses. A line is either a row or a column.
Count rows down from the top and columns across from the left. Both counts start at 1. To find R2C4, go to row 2 and across to column 4.
Number the boxes across the top first, then across the middle, then across the bottom. The top-left box is box 1 and the bottom-right box is box 9.
Two cells that share a house see each other. They can’t hold the same digit. These cells are also called peers.
R2C4 shares row 2 with R2C5 and column 4 with R3C4. It also sees R3C5 through box 2.
The small digits in an empty cell are its candidates. To work them out, start with 1 through 9 and cross off the digits you find in the cell’s three houses.

copy.description: Check R2C4. Row 2 rules out 2, 4, and 9.
copy.reason: Column 4 rules out five more digits, 1, 5, 6, 7, and 8. You’ve already crossed off the digits you see in box 2. Only 3 is left.

paragraphs: Place the 3. A cell with just one candidate gives you a naked single. This can also happen later, after another move lets you cross out a candidate.

blocks.title: Place a single
blocks.instruction: Pick an empty cell with one candidate. Enter that digit.

lessons.title: Full House
lessons.summary: Fill the last empty cell in a house.

paragraphs: Scan rows, columns, and boxes for a house with eight filled cells. Count which digit from 1 to 9 is missing.
If the house has two or more gaps, try a different house.
Look for a house with eight digits filled in. Check which digit from 1 to 9 is missing and put it in the gap.
For a box, count the nine cells inside its thick border. If you find two gaps in a house, check the candidates in each empty cell to see if one has a single choice.

lessons.title: Hidden Single in a Box
lessons.summary: Scan one box for the only place a digit can go.

paragraphs: Choose a digit that is missing from a box. Look at the rows and columns crossing its empty cells. If a row or column already contains that digit, it rules out those cells. When only one cell remains, place the digit there.

items: Start with a digit that already appears several times on the board.
Choose a box where it is missing.
Use matching digits outside the box to rule out rows and columns inside it.
Place the digit only when exactly one cell in the box can contain it.

paragraphs: Beginner puzzles combine this scanning technique with Full House. Easy adds Hidden Singles in rows and columns and Naked Singles, where you work through the candidates of one cell.

groups.title: Easy
groups.overview: Use all singles, including candidates in a cell and missing digits in lines.

lessons.title: Hidden Single
lessons.summary: Place a digit when it has only one possible cell in a house.

paragraphs: Pick a digit that already appears in several boxes. Find a box that still needs it and use the placed copies to rule out rows and columns.
If exactly one empty cell in the box can take the digit, place it there. You can also search one row or column at a time.
Choose a digit a house still needs. Check every empty cell in that house for it. If just one cell can take the digit, put it there. Other candidates in that cell make the single easy to miss.

items: In a row, look for copies of your digit in the crossing columns and boxes.
In a column, check the crossing rows and boxes.
In a box, follow the rows and columns through the box. A placed copy on either line rules out the cells it crosses.

lessons.title: Naked Single
lessons.summary: Place a digit when it’s the only candidate left in its cell.

paragraphs: Start with an empty cell that shares houses with many placed digits. Compare the digits already in its row, column, and box.
If those houses rule out eight different digits, place the one that remains. With candidates shown, look for a cell with one candidate.
Pick an empty cell. Cross off the digits you see in its three houses. One candidate left means you can fill the cell.
Check a cell again after you erase candidates. A pair, for instance, can cut a cell’s two candidates down to one.

groups.title: Medium
groups.overview: Remove candidates using intersections and small sets.

lessons.title: Locked Candidates
lessons.summary: Erase a candidate when its only places in one house are also in another.

paragraphs: Highlight one digit and look for a box where all its candidates line up in one row or column. This is the start of pointing.
For claiming, start with a row or column whose candidates for that digit all fall in one box. Continue if the other house still has the digit as a candidate outside the overlap.
A line crosses three cells of a box. When one house has to put a digit in those three cells, both houses get the digit from that placement.

Check where a digit can go in the box. If all its candidates sit on one line, erase the digit from that line outside the box. Two candidates in the box make a pointing pair. Three make a pointing triple.
Read along a row or column. If all its candidates for your digit sit inside one box, the line has claimed that box’s copy. Erase the digit from the rest of the box.

lessons.title: Naked Subsets
lessons.summary: When several cells have just enough digits to fill them, erase those digits from the rest of the house.

paragraphs: Pick a house with several short candidate lists. Start with two cells that each have the same two candidates.
For a triple or quadruple, add cells whose candidates mostly repeat digits you have already counted. Continue when the number of distinct digits matches the number of cells.
If the cells all sit in the overlap of a line and a box, look for removals in both houses.
Pick cells in one house and count the different digits in their candidate lists. Three cells with only three digits between them have to use all three. The same count works with two or four cells.
Two cells each show only 4 and 6. Whichever takes 4, the other takes 6. Erase 4 and 6 from the rest of the house.
A triple could have cells with 2 and 3, 2 and 5, and 3 and 5. Together they need all of 2, 3, and 5. Erase those digits from the rest of the house.
The lists 12, 24, 34, and 123 contain only four distinct digits. In one house, those four cells take up 1, 2, 3, and 4. Erase the four digits elsewhere in the house.
When both cells sit where a line crosses a box, the pair uses its digits in both houses. Erase them from the other cells of the line and the box.
Three cells can also fill the stretch where a line crosses a box. Erase the triple’s digits in both houses. A quadruple is too large for that three-cell overlap.

lessons.title: Hidden Subsets
lessons.summary: If several digits have only the same few cells available, erase the other candidates from those cells.

paragraphs: In one house, pick a missing digit with only two or three possible cells. Look for other missing digits whose candidates fit inside that same small set of cells.
Continue if the number of cells equals the number of chosen digits. Look inside those cells for candidates outside the chosen digits.
Start with digits a house still needs. Count every cell that can take at least one of your chosen digits. If there are as many cells as digits, those cells are all spoken for.
When two digits can only go in the same two cells, those cells have to take the pair. Check all nine cells of the house before you erase the other candidates in those two cells.
Count the cells that can take any of three digits. If there are exactly three such cells in the house, erase their other candidates. A cell can show any one, two, or all three of the chosen digits.
Try four digits that appear only a few times each. Before you erase the other candidates from their four cells, scan the whole house for another copy of any of the chosen digits.

groups.title: Tricky
groups.overview: Follow one digit across several houses.

lessons.title: X-Wing
lessons.summary: Look for two rows that use the same two columns for a digit, or the same pattern turned sideways.

paragraphs: Pick one digit. Find a row with exactly two places for it and scan the other rows for the same two columns.
A row with a few extra candidates in one box is worth checking for a fin. If a corner is missing, check the sashimi version. You can start with columns as well.
Look for a digit with exactly two places in each of two rows, lined up in the same columns. One row takes one column and the other takes the second. That uses up both columns for this digit.
With a pair of rows, erase the digit from both columns outside those rows. If you spot the rectangle by checking two columns first, erase from the crossing rows outside those columns.

The four corners can come with extra candidates, called fins, outside the crossing lines. All fins must share a box. A target sits in that box on a crossing line, outside the starting lines. If a fin takes the digit, the box rules out the target. If all fins are gone, the X-Wing rules it out.

Set the fins aside and look at what’s left of the rectangle. With a sashimi, one starting line has only one corner left. That corner fixes the digit in one crossing line, and the other starting line uses the second. Check for removals in the same part of the fin box.

lessons.title: Skyscraper
lessons.summary: Find two rows with two places each for a digit and one pair of ends in the same column.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and find two rows with exactly two places each for it. Look for pairs with one column in common and different columns at the other ends.
Continue if another candidate for the digit can see both of those other ends. You can turn the same search sideways.
Pick a digit with two candidates in each of two rows. Find a candidate in one row directly above the matching candidate in the other. The two far ends must sit in different columns.

Only one of the aligned cells can take the digit. At least one row has to put it at its far end. Erase the digit from cells that see both far ends. You can also use two columns with one pair of ends in the same row.

lessons.title: Two-String Kite
lessons.summary: Join a row pair and a column pair for one digit through the box they share.

paragraphs: Find a row with exactly two places for one digit. Look for a column with exactly two places for the same digit.
Continue if one end of each pair shares a box with the other. Check whether another candidate sees both far ends.

Find a row and a column with exactly two places each for the same digit. You need four different cells, with one end from each pair in the same box. Only one of those ends can take the digit, so at least one far end has to take it.

For each kite, erase the digit from cells that see both far ends. A second pair can use the same joining cells in the box. Trace the two kites separately so you use the right far ends for each removal.

lessons.title: Empty Rectangle
lessons.summary: Use a box’s two candidate lines and a pair outside it to erase a candidate.

paragraphs: Pick one digit in a box. Look for candidates that all fit on one row and one column, with candidates on both arms.
Look outside the box for a row or column with only two places for that digit. Continue if one end lines up with an arm of the box.

Pick one digit in a box. All its candidates must fit along one row and one column, with marks on both arms. The four cells off those lines give the pattern its name. The cell where the arms meet can also show the digit.

Find a line outside the box with only two places for the digit. One end of the pair must line up with one arm. If that end takes the digit, the box has to put its copy on the other arm. Look for a target on that other arm’s line that also sees the far end of the pair. Either placement rules it out.

You can start from either arm. If the target and the far end are the only two places for the digit in their line, follow the same argument backwards for a second removal. When the box has just two candidates, you can also read the pattern as a short X-Chain.

lessons.title: Swordfish
lessons.summary: Find a digit that three rows can place only in the same three columns.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and mark the columns it can use in rows with two or three places for it. Start with two rows whose candidates mostly line up.
Look for a third row that fits the same three columns. If some candidates fall outside those columns, keep looking only if those extras share one box. You can also start with columns.

Look across three rows for one digit. Each row must have at least two candidates, and together they can use only three columns. Those rows need three copies in distinct columns. Erase the other candidates in those columns. You can also start with three columns and erase from the crossing rows.

Set aside the candidates outside the crossing lines. If they all sit in one box and you can see an ordinary Swordfish without them, check where the crossing lines enter that box. Erase only outside the starting lines. A fin in the box rules out the target if it takes the digit, and the Swordfish rules it out if all fins are gone.

If at least one starting line has just one candidate once you set the fins aside, you have a sashimi. That candidate fixes one of the three placements. The others still have to use different crossing lines. Look for the same targets as in the finned version.

groups.title: Hard
groups.overview: Recognize wings and other fixed patterns.

lessons.title: XY-Wing
lessons.summary: Either digit in the pivot makes one of the wings take their common digit.

paragraphs: Pick a cell with two candidates. For each of those digits, look for a cell it sees with exactly two candidates, one of which is that digit.
Continue if the two outside cells share the same extra digit. Look for another cell with that digit that sees both outside cells.
In the example, the middle cell, or pivot, has 1 and 2. Look for two cells that see it. One has only 1 and 3 and the other has only 2 and 3. Those two cells are the wings.

A 1 in the pivot leaves the 1 and 3 wing with 3. A 2 leaves the other wing with 3. Erase 3 anywhere that sees both wings. Check each wing against the pivot separately. They can see it through different houses.

lessons.title: XYZ-Wing
lessons.summary: The pivot holds the wings’ common digit, so a target has to see all three cells.

paragraphs: Pick a cell with three candidates. Look for two cells it sees that each contain only two of those three digits.
Continue if the pairs share one digit and together cover all three. A target must have that shared digit and see all three cells.
The pivot in the figure has 2, 8, and 9. The wings see the pivot and have only 2 and 8, or 8 and 9. If the pivot takes 2 or 9, one wing takes 8. The pivot could also take 8 itself.
Erase 8 from a cell that sees all three. R6C5 sees the wing in R2C5 through column 5, and sees the pivot and the other wing through the middle box.

lessons.title: W-Wing
lessons.summary: Link two cells with the same two candidates so one wing must take the other digit.

paragraphs: Find two cells that have the same two candidates. Pick one of those digits and look for a house with exactly two places for it.
Keep looking if each end of that pair sees a different starting cell. A target for the other digit must see both starting cells.
In the figure, both wings have 5 and 7. Column 2 has just two places for 7, and each of those places sees a different wing. Whichever place takes 7 leaves the wing it sees with only 5.
Erase 5 in any cell that sees both wings. If you find a house with two places for 5 instead, use that link to look for a removal of 7.

lessons.title: Jellyfish
lessons.summary: Find a digit that four rows can place only in the same four columns.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and start with rows whose candidates fall in only a few columns. Add rows that reuse those columns.
Check for four rows that use four columns between them. For a finned version, all candidates outside those four columns must share a box. You can also start with columns.

Pick a digit and four rows with at least two candidates each. Count the distinct columns that contain those candidates. If the count is four, those four rows use up the columns for that digit. Erase the other copies in the columns. Four starting columns work the same way.

If you have a Jellyfish plus a few extra candidates outside the crossing lines, check where the extras are. They must all be in one box. The target is in that box and on a crossing line, outside the starting lines. It loses if a fin takes the digit and if the Jellyfish uses up the crossing lines.

When you set the fins aside, one or more starting lines can be left with just one candidate. Those candidates fix some of the placements. All four starting lines still need different crossing lines. Use the same target area as for a finned Jellyfish.

lessons.title: Unique Rectangle
lessons.summary: Look for four corners where swapping two digits would give a second solution.

paragraphs: On a puzzle with one solution, start at a cell with only two candidates. Look for that same pair in a second cell in its row or column.
Look across those lines for two more cells that both contain the pair. Continue if the four corners span exactly two boxes. The extra candidates and strong links tell you which version to use.

Use this on a puzzle with exactly one solution. Look for four empty corners in two rows and two columns, across exactly two boxes. All four can take the same two digits. If they used only those digits, each diagonal would hold one of them. You could swap the two digits without changing which digits any house contains. At least one corner has to use an extra digit to prevent that swap.

blocks.title: Type 1 with extras in one corner

paragraphs: If three corners have only the pair, the fourth has to use an extra digit. Erase both digits of the pair from that corner.

blocks.title: Type 2 with the same extra on adjacent corners

paragraphs: Look for two neighboring corners with the same extra digit and the other two corners with just the pair. One of the two extras must be placed. Erase that digit in any cell that sees both corners with the extra.

blocks.title: Type 3 with a subset of extra digits

paragraphs: Two adjacent corners have extras, and between them they need at least one extra digit. Count the two corners as one slot for those digits. Add cells from a house they share until the number of distinct digits equals the number of slots. Erase those digits from the other cells of that house.

blocks.title: Type 4 with a strong link on one side

paragraphs: Two adjacent corners have extras. Look for a digit of the rectangle pair that has only those two places in a shared house. One corner must take it. If the other corner took the second digit of the pair, all four corners would use only the pair. Erase the second digit from both corners with extras.

blocks.title: Type 5 with the same extra across the diagonals

paragraphs: Find the same extra digit in two opposite corners or in three corners, with no other extras. At least one of those corners must take the extra. Erase it from any cell that sees all the corners where it appears.

blocks.title: Type 6 with one digit locked to a diagonal

paragraphs: The two corners with extras are opposite each other. Find a digit of the pair whose only places in both rows and both columns are the four corners. It must take one whole diagonal. If it took the diagonal with extras, the other two corners would take the second digit and allow the swap. Erase the linked digit from the corners with extras.

Start at a corner that contains just the pair and look at the opposite corner. One digit of the pair must have no places beyond the rectangle in that opposite corner’s row and column. If the opposite corner took the other digit, both lines would force the rectangle into the swappable arrangement. Erase that other digit from the opposite corner.

The swap can also involve digits you’ve already placed. Check that none of the corners is a given. With three filled corners, erase the candidate that would complete the swap. With two filled corners and the same extra candidate in both empty corners, erase that extra from cells that see both empty corners.

The swap has to respect the givens. A rectangle digit might have been crossed out during an earlier move even though the givens allow it there. Check that both digits could go in all four corners from the givens before you use this version.

lessons.title: BUG+1
lessons.summary: In a puzzle with one solution, look for the extra candidate that keeps all the empty cells from having two choices.

paragraphs: Scan the empty cells for short candidate lists. Keep looking if exactly one cell has three candidates and every other empty cell has two.
In the row, column, and box of the three-candidate cell, count the possible spots for each of its digits. Look for the digit that has three spots in all three houses.

BUG stands for Bivalue Universal Grave. In a BUG, every empty cell has two candidates and every missing digit has two places in each house that needs it. If you solved that grid, changing every originally empty cell to its other digit would still leave one of each digit in every house. You’d have two solutions.

For BUG+1, look for one cell with three candidates and two candidates in every other empty cell. In the three-candidate cell, find the digit with three places in each of its houses. If crossing it out leaves a BUG, solving without that candidate would let you swap the choices to make another solution. A one-solution puzzle has to use the extra digit.
Check the counts across the grid before placing it. A cell with three candidates can also occur without a BUG pattern.

lessons.title: Simple Coloring
lessons.summary: Use two colors to follow the possible placements of one digit.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and find a row, column, or box with exactly two places for it. Color the candidates differently.
At each end, look for another house where that digit also has exactly two places. Keep going while you can add links, then check for a conflict within one color or a candidate that sees both.

Find two candidates for the same digit that are the only places for it in one house. Color them differently. When either candidate forms another such pair, color the new end with the opposite color. Within one connected set, placing one color rules out the other.
If an uncolored candidate sees one of each color, it can’t take the digit whichever color is placed. Erase it.

Two candidates of the same color can’t both be placed if they see each other. Erase that color throughout the connected set and place the other color. Give disconnected sets their own colors until you can link them.
Check whether every candidate for the digit in a house would disappear if you placed one color. That would leave the house without the digit. Erase that color and place the other one.

lessons.title: X-Chain
lessons.summary: Follow strong and weak links for one digit to find a candidate that sees both ends.

paragraphs: Pick a digit with exactly two places in a house. From one end, find another candidate for that digit that it sees.
Keep the new candidate if it has a house with a second two-place link. After a strong link, look for an outside candidate that sees both ends.

When a house has just two places for a digit, the pair forms a strong link. If one end is ruled out, the other must be placed. Any two candidates for the same digit that see each other form a weak link. If one end is placed, the other must be ruled out.

Use a strong link at each end of the chain and alternate the links in between. Rule out the first candidate and trace the result. At each solid link, place the next candidate. At each dashed link, rule it out. This forces the final candidate, so a cell that sees both ends loses the digit.
A Skyscraper or Two-String Kite uses three links. You can keep going through more houses as long as the links alternate and the last one is strong.

lessons.title: XY-Chain
lessons.summary: Link cells with two candidates until the same digit appears at both ends.

paragraphs: Start at a cell with two candidates. Pick one digit as the starting end. Use the other digit to find a cell you can see with exactly two candidates that includes it.
Switch to the other digit in each new cell. Continue until a far end has the starting digit and another candidate for that digit sees both ends.

Pick one candidate to cross out in a cell with two marks. That forces its other digit. Find another two-candidate cell that sees the first and shares the forced digit. Cross out that digit there and use the other mark to continue.

Stop when the last cell has to take the digit you first crossed out. One of the two ends has to take it. Erase that digit wherever a cell sees both ends. An XY-Wing uses the same argument with three cells.

lessons.title: 3D Medusa
lessons.summary: Use cells with two candidates to carry two-color reasoning from one digit to another.

paragraphs: Start at a cell with exactly two candidates and give them opposite colors. Pick either digit and look for a house where it has exactly one other spot.
Give that other spot the opposite color. If it is in a cell with two candidates, switch digits there and look for another link. Follow each connected branch.
If a link stops, check the other branches. Look for a conflict within one color or a candidate that either color would rule out.

Color the two places for a digit as in Simple Coloring. When you reach a cell with exactly two candidates, its other mark gets the opposite color. Keep following pairs in houses and in cells. In the connected set, all the candidates of one color can be placed together when that color is true.

blocks.title: When one color breaks a rule

items: One cell would get two digits of the same color.
One house would get two copies of the same digit.
Placing the color would erase every candidate from an empty cell.
Placing the color would leave a house with no place for a missing digit.

paragraphs: Any one of these checks rules out the entire color. Place the candidates of the other color in this set.

blocks.title: When either color rules out the same candidate

items: A cell contains both colors. Both choices for the cell rule out its uncolored candidates.
An uncolored candidate sees its own digit in both colors. It loses whichever color is placed.
An uncolored candidate has one color in its cell and sees its own digit in the other color. Either placement rules it out.

lessons.title: WXYZ-Wing
lessons.summary: Four cells with four digits can force a digit across houses.

paragraphs: Start with a cell that has a short candidate list. Add nearby cells that reuse those digits until four cells contain exactly four distinct digits between them.
For each digit, check whether all its copies in the four cells see one another. Keep the pattern if at least three digits pass this check.

Pick four cells with exactly four different candidates between them. Look at one digit at a time. If all the cells that could take it in the wing see one another, that digit is restricted. Only one of those cells can take it.
An almost locked set (ALS) has one more candidate digit than cells. All its cells share one house.
A common WXYZ-Wing connects two ALSs with four cells in total. This arrangement is a small ALS-XZ pattern.
The whole wing can span several houses. It is not necessarily one ALS.
If three digits are restricted, they can fill at most three cells. The fourth digit has to fill at least one. Erase it from a cell that sees every place it could go in the wing.
R4C3, R4C4, and R4C6 form a three-cell ALS with digits 1, 2, 5, and 9. R6C1 forms another ALS with candidates 1 and 9.
The two 1 candidates share box 4, so the sets cannot both use 1. At least one set must use 9.
R4C2 sees all the 9 candidates in both sets. It therefore loses candidate 9.
The restricted-digit count also explains this removal. It does not require every four-cell arrangement to have the same ALS layout.

All four cells need digits, so when every digit is restricted, each goes in exactly one cell. For each digit, erase it from cells that see all its places in the wing. With two unrestricted digits, this count gives no specific digit to erase.

references.label: Almost Locked Sets (ALS): the shared idea

groups.title: Expert
groups.overview: Construct general alternating inference chains and loops.

lessons.title: Alternating Inference Chains
lessons.summary: Follow alternating links to show that at least one end of the chain must be true.

paragraphs: Start with a strong link. Look for a cell with two candidates or a digit with exactly two places in a house.
From the far end, find a candidate that conflicts with it and has a strong link of its own. Keep alternating. After a strong link, look for a candidate that conflicts with both ends.
For a grouped chain, also look for several spots for one digit in the same stretch of a box and a line. Treat the group as one end.

Use a strong link at both ends and alternate strong and weak links in between. Suppose the first candidate is false. A strong link forces the next candidate to be true, then a weak link makes the next one false. Continue to the last link, which forces the candidate at that end.

blocks.title: Type 1 with the same digit at both ends

paragraphs: If the ends show the same digit, erase it from any cell that sees both. The links in the middle can switch digits.

Suppose the ends are 2 in cell A and 7 in cell B, and the two cells see each other. A 7 in A would cross out the 2 in A and the 7 in B, leaving both ends false. Erase 7 from A. The same reasoning rules out 2 in B if it’s there.

Candidates for one digit where a line crosses a box can act as a single end of a link. The group is true when any member is true. A weak link into the group has to rule out all its members. A strong link can join two groups, or a group and a single candidate, if they cover every place for the digit in a house.

lessons.title: Nice Loops
lessons.summary: Follow a chain back to the same candidate and check the two links that meet there.

paragraphs: Start at a candidate with several links, such as a digit in a cell with two candidates and a two-place link in its row.
Alternate strong and weak links. Continue if a link can return to the original candidate or group. Check whether the first and last links match.
Start at a candidate and alternate strong and weak links until you’re back where you started. The first and last links can be different or the same. The deduction comes from that join.

With two weak links at the join, assume the starting candidate is true. The loop takes you back to that candidate and makes it false, so erase it. With two strong links, starting with it false forces it to be true. Place it.

If the links alternate at the join, pick a weak link and assume one end is false. Follow the rest of the loop to force the other end true. Any candidate that conflicts with both ends can go. Check each weak link separately.
A group stands for at least one of its candidates. When a link makes the group false, all its candidates are false. Trace the rest of the loop to see whether it contradicts the starting assumption.

At least one end of the weak link must be true. When one end is a group, the target has to conflict with every member of that group and with the other end. If both ends are groups, check all the members at both ends.

groups.title: Master
groups.overview: Connect groups of candidates and almost locked sets.

lessons.title: Almost Locked Sets (ALS)
lessons.summary: One extra candidate digit lets a set connect to another set and force a removal.

paragraphs: Start with a cell that has two candidates, or two cells in one house with three distinct candidates. Look for a second set nearby that shares a digit.
Keep the connection if every copy of the shared digit in one set sees every copy in the other. Then look for another shared digit or a link to a third set.
An almost locked set (ALS) contains one more candidate digit than cells. All its cells share one house.
A cell with candidates 2 and 7 is an ALS. Two cells in one row with candidates 1, 2, and 3 between them also form an ALS.

blocks.title: One digit short of a locked subset

paragraphs: A naked pair has two cells and two candidate digits. An ALS with two cells has three candidate digits.
If one digit is absent from an ALS, its cells must use every other digit. The ALS then becomes a locked subset.
For example, two cells in one row contain {1, 2} and {2, 3}. Without 1, they must take 2 and 3.
Two separate ALSs can share a restricted common candidate, called X. Every cell that contains X in one set sees every X cell in the other.
The sets cannot both use X. At least one set must therefore use all its other digits.
If both sets contain another digit Z, at least one set must use Z. If an outside cell sees every Z candidate in both sets, it loses Z.

blocks.title: The shared digits in this example

paragraphs: The column set contains R3C7 and R5C7, with digits 1, 3, and 4. The row set contains R2C4, R2C5, R2C7, and R2C9.
The row set has five candidate digits: 1, 3, 4, 5, and 9. Both sets therefore have one more candidate digit than cells.
Their 3 candidates both lie in column 7, so the sets cannot both use 3. At least one set must use 1.
R2C8 sees every 1 candidate in both sets. It therefore loses candidate 1.

blocks.title: Named patterns in the ALS family

items: ALS-XZ connects two ALSs through a restricted common candidate.
A common WXYZ-Wing is an ALS-XZ pattern with four cells in total. The wing combines ALSs rather than forming one ALS.
ALS-XY-Wing connects three ALSs through two different restricted common candidates.
An ALS Chain connects a sequence of ALSs. Each internal set uses different digits for its incoming and outgoing links.

paragraphs: The names describe different arrangements of the same idea. A forced digit in one ALS restricts the choices in another.

lessons.title: Forcing Chains and Nets
lessons.summary: Follow a possible move until it breaks a rule or leads to the same result as every other choice.

paragraphs: Start at a cell with two candidates or a digit with only two places in a house. A candidate that affects several short candidate lists is also worth a try.

Try a choice and look for a single that follows from it. Keep going while changes force new moves. Look for a rule that breaks or a move that all starting choices share. For a net, record which earlier changes work together to force the next move.

Pick a candidate. Try placing it or crossing it out and track the moves that follow. A placement rules out the other digits in that cell and the same digit in its peers. Whenever a cell or a missing digit in a house has one choice left, follow that placement too.

Stop if a cell loses every candidate, a house runs out of places for a digit, or a candidate has to be both true and false. The starting assumption can’t hold. Erase a candidate if placing it caused the contradiction. Place it if crossing it out caused the contradiction.

blocks.title: All choices lead to the same move

paragraphs: Try each candidate in a cell, each place for one digit in a house, or both possibilities for a single candidate. Follow every choice separately. If they all give the same placement or removal, make that move.

A chain goes from one deduction to the next. A net can use several earlier deductions for a single step. For instance, three separate removals might leave only one place for a digit in a column. Check that each of those removals follows from the same starting assumption before you place the digit.
